question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.
Sejal visits the nearby temple off and on.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Periodically.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "off and on" means happening occasionally or at irregular intervals, not constantly or continuously — i.e., periodically. (कभी-कभी, समय-समय पर)
◦ Example: He still visits his old school off and on.

• Since the temple visits happen now and then rather than at every opportunity, the meaning intended is "periodically" / "occasionally", not a fixed regular schedule.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Constantly means without stopping, all the time — this is opposite to the intermittent sense of "off and on".

• Option 3: Continuously means without any break or interruption — again the opposite of the occasional, broken pattern implied by "off and on".

• Option 4: Regularly means at fixed, predictable intervals (e.g., every day) — "off and on" instead suggests an irregular, unpredictable pattern, so "regularly" is not the best fit.

NOTE

• Other common idioms of frequency tested in SSC: "Once in a blue moon" (very rarely), "Day in and day out" (repeatedly, every day), and "Now and then" (occasionally, a synonym of "off and on").

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct sequence to form a meaningful sentence.
(P) unlock their potential
(Q) empowers individuals to
(O) and shape their future
(R) the power of education
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. RQPO.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule for sentence rearrangement: first identify the part that can stand as the subject of the sentence, then arrange the remaining parts so that the sentence reads as one grammatically complete and meaningful unit.

• Part (R) "the power of education" is a complete noun phrase and works best as the subject of the sentence, so it must come first.

• Part (Q) "empowers individuals to" contains the main verb "empowers" and logically follows the subject "the power of education", since it is education's power that empowers individuals.

• Part (P) "unlock their potential" is the infinitive object of "empowers individuals to", so it must directly follow (Q).

• Part (O) "and shape their future" is joined by "and" to the previous infinitive, continuing the action begun by "unlock their potential", so it comes last.

• Combining in this order gives: "The power of education empowers individuals to unlock their potential and shape their future." — a complete, meaningful sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: QROP is incorrect because it begins with "empowers individuals to", which has no subject before it, making the sentence ungrammatical.

• Option 2: OPRQ is incorrect because it begins with "and shape their future", which cannot start a sentence since "and" needs a preceding clause to connect to.

• Option 4: RPOQ is incorrect because after the subject "the power of education", it jumps straight to "unlock their potential" without the necessary verb "empowers individuals to", breaking the grammatical link between subject and verb.

NOTE

• In parts-rearrangement questions, always locate the part with the main subject and finite verb first — these anchor the sentence and other parts (infinitives, "and"-joined phrases, prepositional phrases) fall into place around them.

• A part beginning with "and", "but", "which", or "that" can never be the first part of a rearranged sentence, since these are connecting/relative words that require something before them.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
Mr. Suman / asked me / to pack / my luggages.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. my luggages.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Luggage" is an uncountable (mass) noun in English — it has no plural form and is never used with "a/an" or with an "-s" ending.

• Rule: Uncountable nouns like luggage, furniture, information, advice, news and baggage take a singular verb and cannot be pluralised; quantity is expressed using words like "some", "a lot of", "a piece of", or "much", not by adding "-s".

• In the given sentence, "my luggages" is grammatically wrong; the correct form is "my luggage".
◦ Corrected sentence: Mr. Suman asked me to pack my luggage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "asked me" is grammatically correct — "ask + object + to-infinitive" is a standard structure.

• Option 3: "to pack" is grammatically correct — it is the infinitive object required after "asked me".

• Option 4: "Mr. Suman" is grammatically correct — it is simply the correctly written proper noun subject of the sentence.

NOTE

• Other common uncountable nouns frequently tested in SSC error-spotting questions: furniture, information, advice, news, scenery, machinery, poetry and knowledge — none of these should ever be used with "-s" or with "a/an".

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A place to park aeroplanes
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Hangar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Hangar" is a large building used to house or park aircraft. (विमान रखने का शेड/गोदाम)
◦ Example: The old fighter jets were kept in a hangar at the edge of the airbase.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Hanger — a device used to hang clothes; it sounds similar to "hangar" but has a completely different meaning, which is why it is a commonly confused pair in SSC exams.

• Option 2: Depot — a place used for storing goods or for housing and maintaining vehicles such as buses and trains, not specifically aeroplanes.

• Option 3: Shed — a small, simple structure usually used to store tools, equipment or small vehicles; too small and generic a term for housing aeroplanes.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophone-like pair: "Hangar" (a shed for aircraft) vs "Hanger" (a device for hanging clothes) — a favourite SSC spelling/vocabulary trap.

• Other one-word substitutes related to places: "Depot" (a store or terminus for vehicles/goods), "Aerodrome/Airport" (a place for aircraft take-off and landing), and "Dockyard" (a place where ships are built or repaired).

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in passive voice.
The baker baked the cake.
option_1: The cake was baked by the baker
option_2: The cake had been baked by the baker.
option_3: The baker has been baking the cake.
option_4: The cake has been baked by the baker.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The cake was baked by the baker.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The baker baked the cake" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the cake" becomes the subject; since it is singular, the auxiliary used is "was"; the verb "baked" becomes its past participle form "baked" (V3); and "the baker" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: The cake was baked by the baker.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "had been baked" is the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense, not the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "has been baking" is an active-voice-like continuous construction and does not correctly convert the given sentence into the passive voice at all.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "has been baked" is the passive form of the Present Perfect Tense, which changes the time frame of the original sentence.

NOTE

• Many V3 (past participle) forms of regular verbs are identical to their V2 (past simple) forms, e.g., baked, cooked, played, walked — students must rely on the auxiliary verb (was/were vs has/have) to identify the correct tense in the passive voice, not just the main verb form.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
The teammates made several jibes at the opponent team members during the interview.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Contradict.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As used in the sentence, "jibe" is popularly known as a noun meaning a mocking or taunting remark, but it is also standard (especially in American English) as a verb meaning "to be in accord or agreement with; to correspond, tally or match". (सहमत होना/मेल खाना)
◦ Example: His account of the accident does not jibe with what the witnesses said.

• Taking the dictionary/thesaurus sense of "jibe" as "to agree, correspond, or be consistent with", its standard antonym is "contradict" — to be inconsistent with, or to go against/oppose.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Consolation means comfort given to someone in distress — it is not the standard listed antonym of "jibe" in this sense.

• Option 2: Mockery is actually closer to a synonym of the "taunt" sense of jibe (a mocking remark), not its antonym, so it cannot be the answer.

• Option 3: Inspiration means the process of being mentally stimulated to do something creative — it is unrelated to the "agree/disagree" sense of "jibe" and is not its recognised antonym.

NOTE

• Do not confuse the two senses of the word: as a noun, "jibe"/"gibe" = a taunt or jeer (synonyms: mockery, taunt, jeer; antonym: compliment, praise); as a verb, "jibe" = to agree or be consistent (synonyms: accord, tally, correspond; antonyms: clash, conflict, differ, contradict). SSC antonym/synonym questions often draw from either sense, so check the option list to see which sense is intended.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Athens was suffering under the rule of a powerful small group that had no concern for the people's welfare.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. an oligarchy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "oligarchy" is a form of government or rule in which power is held by a small, powerful group of people. (कुछ शक्तिशाली लोगों का शासन/अल्पतंत्र)
◦ Example: Critics said the country was really being run as an oligarchy of wealthy business families.

• The underlined segment "a powerful small group" (that rules without concern for people's welfare) is best replaced by the single word "an oligarchy", which precisely names this form of rule.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: a democracy means rule by the people, through elected representatives — the opposite of rule by a small powerful group.

• Option 3: a monarchy means rule by a single king or queen, not by a group.

• Option 4: a missionary refers to a person sent to do religious or charitable work; it has no connection to a form of government at all.

NOTE

• Related terms for forms of government often tested in SSC vocabulary: "Democracy" (rule by the people), "Monarchy" (rule by one hereditary ruler), "Autocracy/Despotism" (rule by one person with absolute power), "Theocracy" (rule by religious authority), and "Anarchy" (absence of government/rule).

question:
Select the correct spelling to fill in the blank.
I often fail to ______ remember someone’s name.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. accurately.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "accurately" — meaning in a precise and exact manner, without errors.

• Spelling key: AC + CU + RATE + LY. Note the double "c", the "u" after it, and the base word "accurate" plus the adverb suffix "-ly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "accuriately" — incorrect; an extra "i" has been wrongly inserted before "ately".

• Option 2: "accuratially" — incorrect; the letters after "accurat" have been jumbled and an extra "i" and "al" wrongly inserted.

• Option 3: "acusatively" — incorrect; this misspells the word entirely, replacing "ccurat" with "cusat", which changes it beyond recognition of "accurately".

NOTE

• The adjective form is "accurate" and the noun form is "accuracy" — remember the double "c" in all three related words (accurate, accurately, accuracy).

• Do not confuse "accurately" with unrelated-sounding words like "accusative" (a grammatical case) — the two only share a superficial similarity in sound.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can rectify the incorrectly spelt word in the following sentence.
I doubt that these lifts can acommodate 100 people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. accommodate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "accommodate" — meaning to provide space or lodging for, or to adjust to fit certain requirements.

• Spelling key: AC + COM + MO + DATE — remember the double "c" and the double "m"; this is one of the most common double-letter spelling traps in English.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "acomodate" is incorrect; both the double "c" and the double "m" have been dropped.

• Option 2: "accommodatte" is incorrect; it wrongly doubles the "t" at the end instead of keeping the correct "-date" ending.

• Option 3: "accomodate" is incorrect; the double "m" is missing (only one "m" is used).

NOTE

• Other frequently misspelt double-letter words tested in SSC: "occurrence", "embarrass", "committee", "recommend" and "accompany" — all commonly lose one of their doubled letters when misspelt.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Dissipate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Spend.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dissipate" means to squander or spend wastefully; to use up (money, energy, or resources) until nothing is left, or to scatter/disperse and disappear. (बर्बाद करना/उड़ा देना)
◦ Example: He dissipated his entire inheritance within a few years of reckless living.

• In the sense of wastefully using up resources, "dissipate" is closest in meaning to "spend" (in the sense of using up or exhausting).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Glorious means splendid or magnificent — unrelated in meaning to "dissipate".

• Option 2: Malicious means having the intention to harm someone — unrelated to "dissipate".

• Option 3: Haste means excessive speed or urgency in doing something — it does not carry the meaning of squandering or dispersing.

NOTE

• "Dissipate" also has a physics/science-related sense: to disperse or vanish gradually, as in "the fog dissipated by noon" or "energy is dissipated as heat".

• Related words: "Squander" and "Fritter away" (to waste money or resources carelessly) are close synonyms of "dissipate" in its wasteful-spending sense.

question: Select the sentence that is expressed in passive voice.
option_2: Children are participating in sand-art competition.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The consignment was delivered yesterday.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — identifying passive voice: A sentence is in the passive voice when its subject is the receiver of the action, and the verb is formed with a form of "be" (is/am/are/was/were/has been/etc.) + the past participle (V3) of the main verb.

• In "The consignment was delivered yesterday", the subject "the consignment" receives the action of delivering; the verb is "was delivered" — the auxiliary "was" plus the past participle "delivered" — which is the standard passive structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "I prefer tea to coffee." is in the active voice — the subject "I" performs the action "prefer".

• Option 2: "Children are participating in sand-art competition." is in the active voice (present continuous) — "are participating" is a continuous verb form, not a passive one, since the subject "children" is doing the action.

• Option 3: "She sketches beautifully." is in the active voice (simple present) — the subject "she" performs the action of sketching.

NOTE

• A common trap: an "is/am/are/was/were + verb-ing" construction (continuous tense) LOOKS similar to passive voice because it uses a "be" verb, but it is NOT passive — passive voice always requires the past participle (V3) form, never the "-ing" form, after the auxiliary.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
This year’s budget is unlikely to pass as law since the president’s proposed budgets typically face a jaundiced eye but this one has gotten even more scepticism.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Resentment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a jaundiced eye" means a biased, cynical, or hostile view of something, often coloured by envy, bitterness or resentment; to view something "with a jaundiced eye" is to view it with suspicion or ill will rather than fairly. (द्वेष/पूर्वाग्रह की दृष्टि से देखना)
◦ Example: He looked at his rival's success with a jaundiced eye.

• The idiom originates from the disease jaundice, which was once believed to make everything appear yellow to the sufferer's eyes — symbolising a distorted, negatively-coloured perception.

• Since the president's budgets typically face resentful, hostile scepticism rather than a fair hearing, "resentment" best captures the meaning of "a jaundiced eye" here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Jealousy refers specifically to envy over someone else's possessions or success — narrower than the general hostile bias meant by "jaundiced eye".

• Option 2: Confidence is the opposite of the suspicious, biased outlook implied by "jaundiced eye".

• Option 4: Good will is a friendly, favourable disposition — directly opposite to the hostile, biased sense of "jaundiced eye".

NOTE

• Other idioms of bias/prejudice tested in SSC: "To have an axe to grind" (to have a personal, selfish reason for doing something), "To be green-eyed" (to be jealous), and "To see through coloured glasses" (to judge with a biased viewpoint).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Dodge
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Avoid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dodge" means to avoid or evade something (a blow, a question, a duty, a person) by a quick, clever movement or trick. (चतुराई से बचना/टालना)
◦ Example: He dodged the question about his resignation by changing the topic.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Force means to compel or make someone do something — this is nearly opposite in spirit to "dodge" (to evade).

• Option 3: Boarding relates to getting onto a vehicle or providing lodging — unrelated in meaning to "dodge".

• Option 4: Amount refers to a quantity of something — unrelated in meaning to "dodge".

NOTE

• Close synonyms of "dodge" frequently tested in SSC: "Evade", "Elude", "Duck" and "Sidestep" — all convey avoiding something skilfully.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
Her behaviour was so ostentatious that it attracted the attention of everyone in the room.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Restrained.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ostentatious" means showy, pretentious, or designed to impress others; displaying wealth, knowledge or behaviour in an exaggerated way to attract attention. (दिखावटी/तड़क-भड़क वाला)
◦ Example: His ostentatious display of wealth at the party made many guests uncomfortable.

• The antonym of a showy, attention-seeking manner is "restrained" — modest, controlled, and free of exaggerated display.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Attractive means pleasing or appealing in appearance — this is not opposite to "ostentatious"; in fact, ostentatious behaviour is often intended to be attractive/eye-catching.

• Option 3: Gentle means mild or tender in manner — it does not directly relate to the "showy vs modest" contrast implied by "ostentatious".

• Option 4: Repulsive means causing strong dislike or disgust — it describes a negative reaction, not the opposite quality (modesty) of "ostentatious".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "ostentatious": flashy, showy, pretentious, gaudy, flamboyant. Antonyms: modest, restrained, understated, unassuming, simple — all frequently tested together in SSC vocabulary sets.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Her remarks were relevant to the discussion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Inappropriate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Relevant" means closely connected or appropriate to the matter at hand; pertinent. (उचित/संगत)
◦ Example: Please keep your answer relevant to the question asked.

• The closest opposite among the given options is "inappropriate" — not suitable or fitting for the matter being discussed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Suitable is close in meaning to "relevant" (fitting, appropriate) — it is a near-synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 3: Introductory means serving as an opening or beginning — unrelated to the "pertinent vs not pertinent" contrast.

• Option 4: Conclusive means serving to settle a question decisively — unrelated to the meaning of "relevant".

NOTE

• The most direct antonym of "relevant" is "irrelevant" — not connected to the matter at hand; among the given options, "inappropriate" is the closest available match to this idea, since something inappropriate to a discussion is also not pertinent to it.

• Common confusion pair: "Relevant" (connected to the topic) vs "Reverent" (showing deep respect) — similar spelling, different meanings.

question: Select the option with the correct use of future tense.
option_1: By next December, I will have been completed six years in this home.
option_2: By next December, I will be completed six years in this home.
option_3: By next December, I will have complete six years in this home.
option_4: By next December, I will have completed six years in this home.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. By next December, I will have completed six years in this home.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes an action that will be completed before a specific point of time in the future ("by next December") — this calls for the Future Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Future Perfect Tense:
◦ Structure: Subject + will/shall + have + V3 (past participle) + Object
◦ Used with time markers such as "by + [future time]".

• Applying the rule: "will have completed" (will + have + V3 of "complete") correctly expresses an action that will be finished by the future time referred to — "by next December".
◦ Correct: By next December, I will have completed six years in this home.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "will have been completed" wrongly adds a passive construction ("been completed"), which does not fit here since "I" is the one doing the completing, not something being completed by someone else.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "will be completed" is Simple Future Passive, which again wrongly treats "I" as the receiver of the action rather than the one completing six years.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "will have complete" uses the base form "complete" instead of the required past participle "completed" after "have" — this is a plain grammatical error.

NOTE

• Future Perfect Tense is commonly signalled by phrases like "by the time", "by next [year/month]", and "before" — always followed by "will have + V3".

• Do not confuse Future Perfect ("will have completed") with Future Perfect Continuous ("will have been completing"), which emphasises the ongoing duration of an action up to a future point.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
Ranjith failed in all his exams as he had been addicted of social media.
option_1: as he had been addicted at
option_2: as he had been addicted on
option_3: as he had been addicted in
option_4: as he had been addicted to
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. as he had been addicted to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — fixed preposition: The adjective "addicted" is always followed by the preposition "to", never "of", "at", "on" or "in".
◦ Correct usage: addicted to (something/someone).
◦ Example: Many teenagers today are addicted to social media.

• Applying the rule to the given sentence: the correct phrase is "as he had been addicted to social media".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "addicted at" is incorrect; "at" is not the fixed preposition used with "addicted".

• Option 2: "addicted on" is incorrect; "on" is not the fixed preposition used with "addicted".

• Option 3: "addicted in" is incorrect; "in" is not the fixed preposition used with "addicted".

NOTE

• Other adjectives with fixed prepositions frequently tested in SSC: "afraid of", "proud of", "good at", "married to", "famous for", and "interested in" — these prepositional combinations must be memorised as fixed pairs.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Lethargic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Active.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Lethargic" means lacking energy or enthusiasm; sluggish, drowsy, and unwilling to move or act. (सुस्त/आलसी)
◦ Example: After the heavy lunch, everyone in the office felt lethargic.

• The direct opposite of feeling sluggish and low on energy is being "active" — energetic and lively.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Languid means slow-moving and lacking energy — this is actually a synonym of "lethargic", not its antonym.

• Option 3: Moderate means average or not extreme — it does not describe a level of energy and so is not the antonym of "lethargic".

• Option 4: Angry describes a strong feeling of displeasure — it is unrelated to the energy level implied by "lethargic".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "lethargic": sluggish, listless, languid, drowsy, torpid. Antonyms: active, energetic, lively, vigorous, dynamic — a frequently tested synonym-antonym cluster in SSC exams.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
The evening time when the sun has just set and it is almost dark.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Dusk.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dusk" refers to the darker stage of twilight, the time in the evening just after sunset when it is not yet fully dark. (संध्याकाल/गोधूलि)
◦ Example: The street lamps come on automatically at dusk.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Night refers to the entire period of darkness after the sky is fully dark, not specifically the moment just after sunset.

• Option 3: Dawn refers to the time when the sun rises in the morning — the opposite end of the day from dusk.

• Option 4: Day break is another term for the early morning when light first appears — again, the opposite of the evening period described.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes for times of day frequently tested in SSC: "Dawn/Daybreak" (sunrise), "Twilight" (the soft light before sunrise or after sunset), "Noon" (midday), and "Midnight" (12 a.m.).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The cynical investors believed in every word the analysts said.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. credulous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Cynical" means distrustful of people's motives; inclined to believe that people act only out of self-interest. (संदेहवादी/अविश्वासी)

• The given sentence states that the investors "believed in every word the analysts said" — this describes people who trust and believe easily, which contradicts the meaning of "cynical" (distrustful). The word that correctly fits this behaviour is "credulous" — too ready to believe things, gullible. (भोला/जल्दी विश्वास करने वाला)
◦ Example: Credulous investors often fall for get-rich-quick schemes without questioning them.

• Since believing every word said is a mark of being credulous, not cynical, the underlined word must be substituted with "credulous" to make the sentence logically consistent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: distrustful is a near-synonym of "cynical" itself and would create the same logical contradiction with "believed in every word" — so it does not fix the sentence.

• Option 3: persuasive means having the power to convince others — it describes the analysts' skill, not the investors' trusting nature, so it does not fit the subject "investors".

• Option 4: credible means believable or trustworthy, and describes a quality of a statement or person, not the trusting disposition of the investors themselves — it does not correctly describe the investors who believe others.

NOTE

• Commonly confused pair: "Credulous" (too willing to believe others; gullible) vs "Credible" (believable, worthy of belief) — the former describes a person's trusting nature, the latter describes a statement's or source's trustworthiness.

• "Cynical" and "credulous" are near-opposites: a cynical person doubts everyone's motives, while a credulous person believes too easily.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Human Development Index (HDI) is a summary (1) _________ of average accomplishment in important areas of human development, (2) _________ living a long and healthy life, being informed and having a good quality of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of the normalised (3) _________ for each dimension. The health component is (4) _________ by life expectancy at birth, while the education dimension is measured by the average number of years of schooling for individuals aged 25 and above, as well as the (5) _________ number of years of schooling for school-age children.

Select the most appropriate answer for blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. assessment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun that means an overall evaluation or measure — the HDI is described as "a summary ___ of average accomplishment in important areas of human development". The word "assessment" (an evaluation or appraisal of something) fits this sense of an overall evaluative summary correctly.

• The sentence structure "a summary [noun] of average accomplishment" needs a noun denoting an evaluative measure, and "assessment" is the only option that conveys this idea of a measured evaluation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: regiment means a large military unit — it is completely unrelated in meaning to a summary evaluation of human development.

• Option 3: involvement means the state of being involved in something — it does not convey the sense of an evaluative measure or summary.

• Option 4: collect is a verb, not a noun, and cannot grammatically follow "a summary" in this slot; it also does not carry the meaning of an evaluation.

NOTE

• In cloze/fill-in-the-blank passages, always check both the grammatical category required (noun/verb/adjective) and the contextual meaning of the surrounding sentence before choosing an option — an option may be the wrong part of speech even if it seems topically related.

• "Predicted" correctly conveys this idea of a projected/anticipated number of years of schooling that current school-age children are expected to complete, as opposed to the already-completed "average number of years of schooling for individuals aged 25 and above" mentioned earlier in the sentence.

Additional Information

• Option 1: accompanied means to go along with someone or something — it does not fit the sense of a projected figure of schooling years.

• Option 2: hypnotised means put into a trance-like state — entirely unrelated to a statistical projection.

• Option 4: neglected means ignored or not given proper attention — it does not convey the sense of a forward-looking projected number.

NOTE

• The passage draws a contrast between two education indicators used in the HDI: the "average years of schooling" already completed by adults (25 and above) and the "predicted/expected years of schooling" that today's school-age children are projected to complete — together forming the education dimension of the HDI.
